name: First Aid and Basic Life Support
description: Educational first-aid and adult BLS learning for health-profession learners. This material is not individual medical advice; current certification training, local protocols, and emergency professionals govern real care.

title: Scene Safety and Emergency Activation
description: Hazard awareness, responder safety, consent, emergency activation, and bystander coordination.

quizzes.question: A crash has left a person beside a busy road; vehicles continue to pass close to the scene. What should a bystander do first?
options: Run into the lane and pull the person away before checking traffic.
Stand behind the vehicle and begin care while cars pass.
Ask the injured person to crawl across the road without help.
Stay clear of traffic, call emergency services, and approach only when the area is made safe.
quizzes.rationale: Traffic is an active hazard that can injure both the responder and patient. Emergency services should be activated while access is made safe.

quizzes.question: A strong chemical odor is coming from a room where someone collapsed. Which response best protects everyone?
options: Do not enter; move others away and alert emergency services or hazardous-material responders.
Hold your breath, enter quickly, and drag the person outside.
Open the door wider and ask an unprotected bystander to enter.
Pour water into the room before approaching the person.
quizzes.rationale: Unknown chemical exposure can incapacitate rescuers; entry requires appropriate training and protective equipment. Isolate the hazard and summon specialized help.

quizzes.question: A person is bleeding and you have disposable gloves available. What is the safest next step before direct contact?
options: Wait for gloves even if the person becomes unresponsive and needs CPR.
Put on suitable gloves and use a barrier while providing care within your training.
Skip gloves because visible blood is unlikely to transmit infection.
Ask the injured person to hold your bare hand away from the wound.
quizzes.rationale: Standard precautions reduce exposure to blood and body fluids. Use barriers when available, while not delaying time-critical lifesaving care when no barrier is immediately accessible.

quizzes.question: A crowd is gathering around an injured person in a place where a weapon may still be present. What should you do?
options: Approach from behind the crowd and begin treatment.
Ask another untrained bystander to search for the weapon.
Move to safety, avoid approaching the threat, and notify emergency responders.
Ask the injured person to crawl toward the crowd.
quizzes.rationale: A continuing violence threat makes the scene unsafe. Rescuers should stay clear until law enforcement or other appropriate responders secure access.

quizzes.question: A worker is lying beside a damaged electrical cable. Which action is safest?
options: Pull the worker away using a metal tool.
Touch the worker’s shoulder to check responsiveness.
Cover the cable with a wet cloth before helping.
Keep clear and have the power isolated by someone qualified before approaching.
quizzes.rationale: A live cable can conduct electricity through the patient and rescuer. Power must be made safe before contact; only trained responders should manage electrical hazards.

quizzes.question: A person is struggling in deep water and you are not trained in water rescue. What is the safest aid?
options: Call emergency services and offer reach-or-throw assistance from a secure position if possible.
Jump in immediately and swim directly toward the person.
Tie a rope around your waist and enter the water alone.
Wait silently until the person reaches shore.
quizzes.rationale: An untrained water entry can create a second victim. Use safe shore-based assistance and activate trained rescue services.

quizzes.question: A driver is trapped in a vehicle after a collision, but there is no fire or immediate danger. What is the best general approach?
options: Remove the seat belt and twist the person toward the door.
Keep the person still, call emergency services, and avoid moving them unless danger makes it necessary.
Pull the person out to make the scene easier to manage.
Ask the person to stand and walk to check for injuries.
quizzes.rationale: Unnecessary movement can worsen a suspected injury. Leave extrication to trained responders unless an immediate hazard requires urgent movement.

quizzes.question: A workplace incident involves several injured people and an ongoing machine hazard. What should the first helper prioritize?
options: Move every injured person through the hazard zone.
Ask coworkers to restart the machine after the scene clears.
Stop others from entering the hazard area and activate emergency response with the location and hazards.
Begin treating the nearest person while the machine continues to run.
quizzes.rationale: Control access and communicate the hazard before care begins. Uncontrolled machinery can create additional casualties and compromise rescuers.

quizzes.question: You are alone with an unresponsive person who is not breathing normally. A phone is available. Which action best links response and care?
options: Leave the person to search for several people before calling.
Send an unknown bystander to call while you wait without assessing breathing.
Carry the person outside before activating emergency response.
Call emergency services on speaker, follow dispatcher guidance, and begin CPR as directed.
quizzes.rationale: Early emergency activation and CPR are both time-critical. A speakerphone lets a lone rescuer communicate while staying with the person.

quizzes.question: A bystander says, “Someone should call an ambulance,” but no one moves. What is the best delegation?
options: Point to one person, say “Call emergency services now,” and ask them to confirm when connected.
Repeat the request to the whole crowd and begin waiting.
Ask several people to call without assigning anyone specifically.
Ask the injured person to find a phone.
quizzes.rationale: Direct assignments reduce diffusion of responsibility. Confirming completion ensures the emergency call was actually placed.

quizzes.question: A responsive adult appears injured but is alert and can answer questions. How should a helper begin?
options: Take the person’s belongings to look for medical information.
Introduce yourself, explain the help you can provide, and ask permission before assisting.
Begin examining the person without speaking to save time.
Ask a companion to consent even though the adult can decide.
quizzes.rationale: A capable adult should be involved in decisions about assistance. Clear explanation and consent respect autonomy and improve cooperation.

quizzes.question: A person is unresponsive after collapsing and has no companion nearby. What should a bystander do about consent?
options: Assume the person refused help because they are not answering.
Search the person’s phone before calling emergency services.
Treat the apparent emergency as implied consent for necessary basic assistance while activating emergency services.
Wait indefinitely for a family member to authorize any help.
quizzes.rationale: Unresponsiveness prevents an immediate decision, and delay can be dangerous. Local laws vary, but emergency assistance is generally based on implied consent in this situation.

quizzes.question: A helper notices a strong gasoline smell and a person near a damaged vehicle. Which action is safest?
options: Use a phone beside the fuel spill to call.
Light a flare to help responders see the scene.
Move the vehicle before assessing the hazard.
Keep people away from ignition sources and call emergency services from a safe location.
quizzes.rationale: Fuel vapor can ignite, so avoid ignition sources and maintain distance. Alert responders with the location and hazard details.

quizzes.question: A person has a visible injury and several people are filming. What should the helper do?
options: Ask bystanders to give space and protect the person’s privacy while care is provided.
Allow filming so the crowd can later review the injury.
Post the person’s name and condition to request advice.
Take a close-up photograph before emergency responders arrive.
quizzes.rationale: Crowding and exposure can undermine dignity and interfere with assistance. Share information only with people who need it for the response.

quizzes.question: You arrive at a building where smoke is coming from the entrance and people are shouting for help. What should you do?
options: Open windows and enter before firefighters arrive.
Stay out of the smoke, call emergency services, and direct people away from the building.
Enter briefly while holding your breath to locate the caller.
Ask an unprotected bystander to search each room.
quizzes.rationale: Smoke inhalation can quickly incapacitate rescuers. Fire response requires trained personnel and protective equipment.

quizzes.question: A person is found during a thunderstorm in an exposed field. What should the helper prioritize?
options: Stand under the tallest isolated tree.
Use a metal fence as a handhold while assessing the person.
Move to safer shelter if it can be done without increasing danger, and contact emergency services.
Stay in the open beside the person until the storm passes.
quizzes.rationale: Lightning and weather can injure rescuers as well as patients. Choose safer shelter without creating additional danger and activate help as needed.

quizzes.question: A person in a public place asks you not to call anyone, but then becomes unresponsive. What is the safest response?
options: Honor the earlier request and leave without checking further.
Ask the crowd to decide whether the person needs help.
Delay the call until the person becomes responsive again.
Activate emergency services and provide appropriate basic assistance while monitoring the person.
quizzes.rationale: A new loss of responsiveness signals a potentially life-threatening emergency. Emergency activation is appropriate when the person cannot communicate and may be seriously ill.

quizzes.question: A helper is unsure whether a scene is safe because a damaged power line is nearby. What should they do?
options: Keep a safe distance and wait for qualified responders to isolate the electrical hazard.
Test the line with a stick from close range.
Ask the injured person to confirm whether it is live.
Approach in rubber-soled shoes and touch the person.
quizzes.rationale: A damaged line must be treated as energized until qualified responders make it safe. Improvised testing is dangerous.

quizzes.question: A dispatcher asks for the exact location and callback number. What should the caller provide first?
options: Only the injured person’s name and age.
The location and callback number, then the nature of the emergency and known hazards.
The caller’s opinion about the diagnosis before giving a location.
A long account of events before stating where help is needed.
quizzes.rationale: Dispatchers need location and callback details to send help and reconnect if the call drops. Concise hazard information supports a safer response.

quizzes.question: An injured person is responsive and asks you not to share their details with onlookers. What should you do?
options: Post an update online without identifying yourself.
Share a photograph with coworkers after the emergency ends.
Limit discussion to responders and people directly involved in the person’s care.
Tell the crowd the person’s medical history to organize help.
quizzes.rationale: Privacy remains important during an emergency. Necessary details should be shared only with those who need them to provide assistance.

studyNotes.title: Make the Scene Safe
studyNotes.summary: A helper should identify hazards before approaching and should not become another casualty.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Before approaching
Scan for traffic, fire, electricity, chemicals, violence, unstable structures, and environmental hazards. Stay outside danger zones and request trained responders when a hazard cannot be controlled safely.

### Protect and assist
Use appropriate barriers when available, ask for consent when the person is responsive, and activate emergency services early when the situation is life-threatening.
keyPoints: Pause and scan for hazards before touching anyone.
Do not enter a scene that requires specialized rescue equipment.
Use gloves or other suitable barriers when available.
Prevent additional people from entering the hazard area.
mnemonics: Scan first, then step in.

studyNotes.title: Call for the Right Help
studyNotes.summary: Early activation brings trained responders and equipment while care begins within the helper’s training.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Activate help
Give the location first, describe the number of people and immediate hazards, and state what is happening. Follow dispatcher instructions and keep the line open if requested.

### Delegate clearly
Point to one person and assign one task, such as calling emergency services or bringing an AED. Confirm that the task was completed rather than assuming someone else will do it.
keyPoints: Give a precise location and callback number.
Describe hazards and the number of injured people.
Assign tasks to named people and confirm completion.
Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
mnemonics: Point, name, task, confirm.

studyNotes.title: Consent and Privacy
studyNotes.summary: Respect, consent, and privacy are part of safe first aid.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Consent
Explain who you are and what help you propose. Ask permission from a responsive adult. When a person is unresponsive or unable to decide during an apparent emergency, emergency assistance is generally treated as implied consent, subject to local rules.

### Respect and privacy
Share personal details only with responders who need them. Do not photograph or post the person’s information.
keyPoints: Introduce yourself and explain proposed help.
Ask a responsive person for permission before assisting.
Do not delay emergency activation while seeking consent from an unresponsive person.
Protect the person’s privacy.
mnemonics: Explain, ask, respect.

title: Initial Assessment and Responsiveness
description: Recognizing immediate threats, checking responsiveness and breathing, and deciding when to activate emergency care.

quizzes.question: A person collapses, does not respond to a shout or tap, and has occasional gasps. What should a lay responder recognize?
options: Gasping confirms normal breathing, so observation alone is enough.
The person is asleep and should be left undisturbed.
The gasps show that the airway is clear and no help is needed.
The person may be in cardiac arrest; activate emergency response and begin CPR as directed.
quizzes.rationale: Occasional gasps are not normal breathing in suspected cardiac arrest. Treat the collapse as an emergency and follow dispatcher or training guidance.

quizzes.question: A responsive patient is alert and breathing comfortably after a minor fall. Which position is generally appropriate while you ask what happened?
options: Let the person remain in a comfortable position and avoid unnecessary movement.
Force the person to lie flat even if that worsens breathing.
Ask the person to stand immediately to test balance.
Place the person face-down so they cannot see the injury.
quizzes.rationale: An alert person who is comfortable can usually remain in that position while assessed. Unnecessary movement may aggravate pain or injury.

quizzes.question: A person becomes unresponsive but is breathing normally and has no obvious injury. What should a trained helper consider while emergency help is arranged?
options: Shake the person repeatedly to maintain alertness.
Use a recovery position if appropriate to training and monitor breathing continuously.
Leave the person flat on their back and walk away to find supplies.
Give water to test whether swallowing is intact.
quizzes.rationale: The recovery position may help maintain an open airway in an unresponsive person who is breathing normally. Continue monitoring and follow dispatcher or local training guidance.

quizzes.question: A person reports sudden facial droop and weakness that began about 20 minutes ago. Which information is most useful to relay?
options: A list of all foods eaten in the past week before calling.
Only the person’s age, without describing symptoms.
The observed symptoms and the time they were first noticed, while activating emergency services.
The person’s suspected diagnosis as a certainty and a guessed onset time.
quizzes.rationale: Symptom onset time is important for urgent clinical assessment. Report what you observed rather than presenting an unconfirmed diagnosis.

quizzes.question: A patient with chest discomfort becomes pale and confused. What is the safest priority?
options: Wait to see whether the discomfort resolves over the next hour.
Offer a meal and ask the person to walk around.
Drive the person yourself without considering emergency activation.
Activate emergency services promptly and monitor responsiveness and breathing.
quizzes.rationale: New confusion and pallor with chest discomfort can indicate a serious emergency. Prompt professional assessment is safer than delaying for symptom observation.

quizzes.question: A person is unresponsive and is not breathing normally; a bystander starts CPR. What should another helper do if available?
options: Call emergency services, get an AED, and follow dispatcher instructions.
Ask the CPR provider to stop until a family member arrives.
Search the person’s belongings before contacting help.
Move the person to a different room before calling.
quizzes.rationale: CPR and emergency activation should proceed without avoidable delay. An AED can support early defibrillation when indicated.

quizzes.question: A person is alert but has severe difficulty breathing and asks to sit upright. What should the helper do?
options: Ask the person to walk to a nearby clinic alone.
Allow a position that eases breathing, activate emergency services, and monitor for change.
Make the person lie flat because all first aid begins that way.
Give food and drink to reduce anxiety.
quizzes.rationale: Breathing difficulty is urgent, and comfort positioning may help while responders are summoned. Do not force a position that worsens symptoms.

quizzes.question: A helper sees a person with a major open wound but does not know the cause. Which first step is appropriate?
options: Remove any embedded object to inspect the wound.
Ask the person to clean the wound with household chemicals.
Check scene safety, use a barrier if available, and address severe bleeding while help is activated.
Delay care until the exact diagnosis and cause are known.
quizzes.rationale: Immediate threats can be managed before a diagnosis is known. Severe bleeding requires prompt attention and professional help.

quizzes.question: A person is unresponsive but appears to be breathing normally. What should the helper avoid?
options: Calling emergency services and describing the breathing pattern.
Following dispatcher advice and checking for changes.
Using an appropriate recovery position if trained and safe.
Leaving the person alone without monitoring or arranging emergency assessment.
quizzes.rationale: An unresponsive person can deteriorate quickly. Continuous observation and emergency evaluation are important even when breathing is initially present.

quizzes.question: A bystander finds an unconscious person after a possible fall. Which handling choice is safest before emergency responders arrive?
options: Avoid moving the person unnecessarily unless an immediate hazard requires it.
Sit the person upright to check for back pain.
Pull both arms to assess shoulder movement.
Ask another bystander to carry the person to a car.
quizzes.rationale: A serious injury may involve the head, neck, or spine. Unnecessary movement can worsen harm; immediate hazards may require a different response.

quizzes.question: A person is awake but suddenly cannot speak clearly and one arm drifts downward. What should the helper do?
options: Ask the person to drive to a hospital.
Activate emergency services and note the time the symptoms began or were last known normal.
Give the person food to test swallowing before calling.
Wait for symptoms to become more obvious.
quizzes.rationale: Sudden speech and arm changes may signal a time-sensitive emergency. Call promptly and record symptom timing without delaying help.

quizzes.question: A person with diabetes is awake, confused, and sweating. The cause is not yet known. What should the helper do first?
options: Ask the person to walk until the confusion clears.
Assume the person is intoxicated and leave them alone.
Assess responsiveness and breathing, activate appropriate help, and avoid giving anything by mouth if swallowing is uncertain.
Pour a sugary drink into the person’s mouth immediately.
quizzes.rationale: Confusion can impair safe swallowing and may have multiple causes. Protect the airway, seek appropriate help, and follow training or dispatcher guidance.

quizzes.question: A patient has had a seizure and is now breathing normally but remains drowsy. What is an appropriate first-aid approach?
options: Restrain the person’s limbs to prevent another seizure.
Put a hard object between the teeth.
Give water while the person is drowsy.
Protect the person from nearby hazards, monitor breathing, and seek emergency help when indicated.
quizzes.rationale: Restraint and objects in the mouth can cause injury. After a seizure, monitor and protect the person while following local guidance and emergency criteria.

quizzes.question: A person is responsive but appears pale, sweaty, and weak after an injury. What should the helper do?
options: Activate emergency services, keep the person comfortable and warm, and monitor for deterioration.
Give a large meal and ask them to stand.
Leave them alone to recover without reassessment.
Apply ice directly to the chest and neck.
quizzes.rationale: Pallor, sweating, and weakness after injury can accompany serious illness or shock. Prompt help, warmth, and observation are safer than food or exertion.

quizzes.question: A person’s breathing changes from normal to absent while you are waiting with them. What should you do?
options: Move the person to a chair before taking action.
Tell dispatch immediately and begin CPR or follow dispatcher instructions.
Continue the same observation plan because help was already called.
Give the person water to stimulate breathing.
quizzes.rationale: A sudden breathing change is a critical deterioration. Update dispatch and start appropriate resuscitation steps without delay.

quizzes.question: A helper is uncertain whether a person’s breathing is normal. What is the safest response when the person is unresponsive?
options: Wait several minutes to see if breathing improves.
Ask the person to speak before checking further.
Treat the situation as urgent, activate emergency services, and follow dispatcher or CPR-training guidance.
Assume breathing is normal unless the person turns blue.
quizzes.rationale: Unresponsiveness with uncertain or abnormal breathing may represent a life-threatening emergency. Prompt activation and guided action are safer than waiting for late signs.

quizzes.question: A person with a suspected spinal injury is alert and breathing without distress. What is the best general approach?
options: Ask them to sit and rotate the neck to identify pain.
Pull them upright by both arms.
Test walking before deciding whether to call for help.
Ask the person to remain still in a comfortable position and await trained responders.
quizzes.rationale: Unnecessary movement can worsen a serious injury. Keep the person still and activate emergency response when significant trauma is suspected.

quizzes.question: A person is unresponsive and breathing normally after a possible overdose. Which response is best?
options: Activate emergency services, monitor breathing continuously, and use naloxone only if available and within training.
Leave the person to sleep because normal breathing rules out danger.
Give a drink to wake the person.
Induce vomiting before calling for help.
quizzes.rationale: Overdose can worsen despite initially present breathing. Continuous monitoring and emergency assessment are appropriate; use any medication only according to training and directions.

quizzes.question: A patient has a serious injury and asks, “Am I going to be okay?” What is the best communication?
options: Describe frightening possibilities in detail.
Speak calmly, explain that help is coming, and avoid promises you cannot verify.
Promise there is no serious injury before assessment.
Tell the person to stop asking questions.
quizzes.rationale: Calm, honest reassurance supports cooperation without making unsupported claims. Share clear updates and stay with the person when safe.

quizzes.question: A person has severe pain and becomes increasingly drowsy. What should the helper do?
options: Offer food and medication from another person’s bag.
Encourage the person to walk to stay awake.
Reassess responsiveness and breathing, activate or update emergency services, and monitor closely.
Assume sleep will relieve the pain and leave.
quizzes.rationale: Increasing drowsiness can signal deterioration. Reassessment and emergency communication are more important than exertion or unsupervised medication.

studyNotes.title: A Structured First Look
studyNotes.summary: A brief, organized assessment helps identify life-threatening problems without delaying help.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### First look
Check scene safety, responsiveness, and whether breathing appears normal. A person who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs urgent emergency response. Gasping is not normal breathing.

### Continue observing
Watch for changes, communicate findings to dispatchers, and stay within your training. A helper does not need to diagnose the cause before activating emergency services.
keyPoints: Check safety before approaching.
Assess responsiveness and normal breathing.
Treat gasping as abnormal breathing in a suspected arrest.
Activate emergency response promptly for severe signs.
mnemonics: Safe, response, breathing, call.

studyNotes.title: Position and Ongoing Observation
studyNotes.summary: Positioning should support breathing and safety while a person awaits professional help.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Choose position carefully
If an alert person can breathe comfortably, let them choose a comfortable position. Avoid unnecessary movement when serious injury is suspected. If an unresponsive person is breathing normally and has no concern that prevents movement, the recovery position may help maintain an open airway; follow local training and dispatcher advice.

### Reassess
Observe breathing and responsiveness continuously. If breathing becomes absent or abnormal, update emergency services and follow CPR guidance.
keyPoints: Do not force a comfortable responsive person to lie flat.
Avoid unnecessary movement with suspected serious injury.
Recheck breathing and responsiveness while waiting.
Escalate if breathing becomes abnormal.
mnemonics: Position for comfort, reassess for change.

studyNotes.title: Recognize When Help Is Urgent
studyNotes.summary: Some findings require rapid emergency activation rather than watchful waiting.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Red flags
Examples include unresponsiveness, abnormal breathing, severe bleeding, signs of stroke, chest discomfort with collapse, severe allergic reaction, and major trauma. Call emergency services when a life-threatening condition is suspected.

### Share observations
Describe what you saw and when it began. Avoid stating a diagnosis when you are unsure; precise observations help dispatchers and clinicians.
keyPoints: Unresponsiveness or abnormal breathing is urgent.
Severe bleeding and major trauma need prompt help.
Note the time symptoms began when known.
Report observations rather than guessing a diagnosis.
mnemonics: Describe what you see, when it began.

title: Adult CPR and AED
description: Recognition of adult cardiac arrest, high-quality CPR, AED use, and coordination with emergency response.

quizzes.question: A gym member collapses suddenly, does not respond, and is only gasping. What should a nearby trained helper do first?
options: Place the person on their side and wait for breathing to become normal before calling.
Give the person water and check again after several minutes.
Activate emergency services, begin adult CPR according to training, and send someone to bring an AED.
Activate emergency services and begin CPR based on dispatcher or current training guidance.
quizzes.rationale: Unresponsiveness with absent or abnormal breathing may indicate cardiac arrest. Rapid CPR and AED use offer the best chance while emergency responders are coming.

studyNotes.title: Recognize and respond to suspected arrest
studyNotes.summary: Unresponsiveness with absent or abnormal breathing is an emergency. Activate the emergency response system, begin CPR when indicated, and use an AED as soon as available.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Recognition
For an adult who suddenly collapses, check responsiveness and assess whether breathing is normal. Gasping or irregular gasps are not normal breathing.

### Response
Call emergency services and send someone for an AED. Start CPR according to current training; use an AED promptly and follow its voice prompts. Resume compressions immediately after a shock or a no-shock instruction.
keyPoints: Treat unresponsiveness with absent or abnormal breathing as a possible arrest.
Activate emergency response and request an AED.
Begin CPR and minimize unnecessary interruptions.
Follow AED prompts and resume CPR promptly.
mnemonics: Unresponsive + not breathing normally: call, compress, AED.

studyNotes.title: Compression quality
studyNotes.summary: Effective adult CPR uses a steady rate and adequate depth while allowing full chest recoil and limiting pauses.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Adult compressions
For trained rescuers, current AHA adult BLS guidance uses a compression rate of 100–120 per minute and a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm), while avoiding excessive depth beyond 2.4 inches (6 cm). Allow full recoil and keep interruptions as short as possible.

### Teamwork
When another trained rescuer is available, coordinate role changes to reduce fatigue and keep compressions effective. Follow dispatcher guidance and the rescuer’s current course.
keyPoints: Aim for 100–120 compressions per minute.
Compress at least 2 inches (5 cm), avoiding excessive depth.
Allow the chest to return fully after each compression.
Limit pauses and coordinate rescuer changes.
mnemonics: Rate, depth, recoil, fewer pauses.

studyNotes.title: AED use and team coordination
studyNotes.summary: An AED analyzes heart rhythm and gives instructions; helpers should expose the chest, follow prompts, and keep everyone clear during analysis and shock.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Apply the AED
Turn it on and follow its prompts. Place pads on a bare chest as shown on the pads; ensure no one touches the person during analysis or shock.

### After analysis
Deliver a shock only when the AED directs it. Immediately resume CPR when prompted, and continue until the person shows signs of life, trained responders take over, or the scene becomes unsafe.
keyPoints: Turn on the AED and follow its voice and visual prompts.
Keep everyone clear during analysis and shock.
Resume CPR promptly when the AED directs it.
mnemonics: Power on, pads on, clear, follow prompts.

studyNotes.title: Recognize severity
studyNotes.summary: A person who can cough forcefully, speak, or breathe may have a mild obstruction. A person unable to speak, breathe, or cough effectively needs immediate help.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Mild obstruction
Encourage a responsive person with an effective cough to keep coughing and watch closely. Do not interfere if airflow remains adequate.

### Severe obstruction
If the person cannot speak, breathe, or cough effectively, activate emergency services and provide age-appropriate choking first aid within your current training.
keyPoints: An effective cough can move an object.
Inability to speak, breathe, or cough effectively is severe.
Call emergency services for severe obstruction.
Watch for a change in responsiveness or breathing.
mnemonics: Can cough: encourage; cannot speak/breathe: act.

studyNotes.title: Responsive adult with severe choking
studyNotes.summary: Current AHA/Red Cross first aid guidance recommends cycles of five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts for a responsive adult with severe choking, repeating until relief or the person becomes unresponsive.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### First aid steps
For a responsive adult with severe choking, provide cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts, repeating as needed and consistent with training. If pregnancy or body size prevents abdominal thrusts, use chest thrusts according to current training.

### Avoid harm
Do not perform blind finger sweeps. Stop when the obstruction clears or the person becomes unresponsive, and seek medical assessment as appropriate.
keyPoints: Use 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts.
Repeat cycles until the obstruction clears or the person becomes unresponsive.
Use chest thrusts when abdominal thrusts are not appropriate.
Never do a blind finger sweep.
mnemonics: Five and five; reassess each cycle.

studyNotes.title: If the person becomes unresponsive
studyNotes.summary: If a choking person becomes unresponsive, lower them safely, activate emergency services, and begin CPR; remove an object only if it is visible when opening the airway.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Unresponsive person
Carefully lower the person to a firm surface, activate emergency services, and start CPR according to training. When opening the airway, remove an object only if it is visible; do not sweep blindly.

### After relief
A person who received thrusts or had a severe obstruction may need medical assessment, especially if symptoms persist or injury is possible.
keyPoints: Begin CPR when the person becomes unresponsive.
Look for an object when opening the airway.
Remove only an object that is clearly visible.
Seek medical assessment after a serious episode or ongoing symptoms.
mnemonics: Unresponsive: CPR; visible object only.

studyNotes.title: Control serious bleeding
studyNotes.summary: Prompt, firm direct pressure is a first-line response to serious external bleeding. Emergency services should be activated for severe or uncontrolled bleeding.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Direct pressure
Use gloves or a barrier when available. Apply firm, steady pressure with clean gauze or cloth. If blood soaks through, add material without removing the original dressing.

### Serious bleeding
Activate emergency services for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding. A tourniquet may be used for life-threatening limb bleeding only when available and the helper is trained; follow device instructions and do not loosen it.

Call emergency services for severe or uncontrolled bleeding.

Do not remove a soaked dressing; add layers and maintain pressure.

studyNotes.title: Wound care and infection prevention
studyNotes.summary: Simple wound care uses clean barriers, gentle rinsing when appropriate, and medical assessment for serious, contaminated, or worsening wounds.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Minor wounds
After bleeding is controlled, use clean water to rinse a minor wound and cover it with a clean dressing. Avoid putting harsh chemicals into tissue.

### When to seek care
Deep, gaping, contaminated, bite-related, or persistently bleeding wounds need professional assessment. Watch for increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pain, or drainage.
keyPoints: Use a clean barrier when contacting blood.
Rinse minor wounds with clean water after bleeding is controlled.
Cover with a clean dressing.
Seek professional care for deep, contaminated, bite-related, or worsening wounds.

studyNotes.title: Possible shock
studyNotes.summary: Pale, cool, clammy skin, weakness, confusion, or rapid deterioration after injury may indicate shock and require urgent emergency care.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Recognize and respond
Shock can follow serious injury or illness. Activate emergency services, help the person rest in a comfortable position, keep them from getting cold or overheated, and monitor responsiveness and breathing.

### Avoid unsafe steps
Do not give food or drink to someone with serious injury or altered responsiveness. Do not delay emergency activation while trying home remedies.
keyPoints: Call emergency services for suspected shock.
Keep the person comfortable and monitor closely.
Protect the person from becoming cold or overheated.
Avoid food or drink when serious injury or altered responsiveness is present.

studyNotes.title: Thermal burns
studyNotes.summary: Stop the burning process and cool a thermal burn with cool running water when available; avoid ice and household substances.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Immediate care
Move away from the heat source if safe. Cool the burn with clean, cool running water; remove jewelry or clothing near the burn if it is not stuck. Do not apply ice, butter, toothpaste, or creams as a substitute for assessment.

### Cover and escalate
Cover loosely with a clean, dry dressing. Seek urgent professional care for large, deep, facial, hand, genital, joint, chemical, or electrical burns and for breathing problems.

Do not apply ice or household remedies.
Cover loosely and seek care for serious burns.

studyNotes.contentMarkdown:

### Seek help
A visible deformity, severe pain, loss of function, numbness, or major swelling warrants prompt medical assessment. Keep checking circulation and sensation only within your training.

Do not force a deformed limb straight.
Avoid testing a painful injury by making the person walk.
Get medical assessment for suspected fracture or serious symptoms.

studyNotes.title: Recognize time-sensitive symptoms
studyNotes.summary: Sudden chest pressure, stroke signs, severe breathing difficulty, or rapidly worsening symptoms require prompt emergency activation.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Call early
Do not wait for symptoms to become severe when a heart attack or stroke is suspected. Report symptom onset and changes to emergency dispatch. Use FAST as a simple stroke warning aid: face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty, time to call.

### Support
Keep the person at rest, monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow dispatcher instructions. Do not drive an unstable person yourself if emergency services are available.
keyPoints: Call emergency services promptly for possible heart attack or stroke.
Note when symptoms began or when the person was last known well.
Keep the person at rest and monitor them.
Follow dispatcher instructions.
mnemonics: FAST: face, arm, speech, time to call.

studyNotes.title: Breathing, allergy, and seizure emergencies
studyNotes.summary: Help the person use their own prescribed emergency medication when appropriate and within training, and activate emergency help for severe symptoms.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Breathing difficulty and allergy
Help a person use their own prescribed inhaler or epinephrine auto-injector if available and within your training; follow the device directions and local protocol. Severe breathing difficulty or anaphylaxis requires emergency services.

### Seizure
Protect the person from nearby hazards, cushion the head if possible, and time the seizure. Do not restrain them or put anything in the mouth. Call emergency services for a first seizure, prolonged seizure, repeated seizures, injury, or breathing problems.
keyPoints: Activate emergency services for severe breathing difficulty or suspected anaphylaxis.
Assist with the person’s own prescribed medication only within training.
During a seizure, clear hazards and protect the head.
Never restrain a person or put objects in their mouth during a seizure.
mnemonics: Clear space, protect, time; nothing in the mouth.

### Low blood sugar concern
If a person is awake, able to swallow, and has a known low blood sugar episode, follow their care plan or local first-aid training. If they are confused, seizing, or unable to swallow, call emergency services and give nothing by mouth.

### Poisoning
Contact emergency services or the local poison center promptly. Do not induce vomiting or give home remedies unless a qualified professional directs it. Keep the container or substance information for responders when safe.
keyPoints: Give nothing by mouth to a person who cannot swallow safely.
Call emergency services for severe or altered responsiveness.
Do not induce vomiting after a suspected poisoning.
Share the substance and timing with qualified responders.
mnemonics: If unsafe to swallow: nothing by mouth; call.

studyNotes.title: Monitor and reassess
studyNotes.summary: First aid continues while waiting for help: reassess responsiveness and breathing, watch for change, and report deterioration.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Ongoing checks
Stay with the person when safe. Recheck responsiveness and breathing, note changes, and update emergency dispatch. If breathing becomes abnormal or stops, follow CPR training and dispatcher instructions.

### Comfort and safety
Help the person rest in a position they can tolerate. Keep them warm and protect their privacy. Do not give food, drink, or medication unless it is appropriate, safe, and within training.
keyPoints: Stay with the person when safe.
Recheck responsiveness and breathing.
Report deterioration to emergency dispatch.
Follow CPR training if breathing becomes abnormal or stops.
mnemonics: Stay, reassess, update.

studyNotes.title: Recovery position and airway awareness
studyNotes.summary: A person who is unresponsive but breathing normally may need a position that helps maintain an open airway, provided injury concerns do not make movement unsafe.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Positioning
For an unresponsive person who is breathing normally and has no suspected spinal injury, trained first aid may use a recovery position to help keep the airway clear. Continue monitoring breathing.

### Exceptions
If trauma or spinal injury is suspected, minimize movement and follow dispatcher instructions. If breathing is not normal, prioritize emergency activation and CPR rather than placing the person in a recovery position.
keyPoints: Check that breathing is normal before considering recovery positioning.
Avoid unnecessary movement if spinal injury is suspected.
Continue monitoring after positioning.
Use CPR response rather than recovery positioning when breathing is abnormal.
mnemonics: Normal breathing first; injury concerns guide movement.

studyNotes.title: Clear handoff to responders
studyNotes.summary: A concise handoff includes what happened, when it began, observed changes, first aid given, and relevant known information.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### What to report
Tell responders the person’s symptoms, approximate start time, changes, relevant known conditions or medications if provided, and what first aid was given. State uncertainties clearly rather than guessing.

### Respect and continuity
Keep the scene accessible, protect privacy, and stay available for questions. Do not delay care to collect information that is not immediately available.
keyPoints: Describe the event and symptom timeline.
Report changes and first aid performed.
Share only known information and identify uncertainty.
Do not delay urgent care to gather nonessential details.
mnemonics: What happened, when, what changed, what you did.
